analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over federal grazing land management, including environmental reviews and water projects.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced, sent to the Senate Energy Committee, and never became law; it drew a hearing but no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let a governor ask the federal government to hand over management of grazing land on BLM and Forest Service property. The state would issue 30-year grazing permits, run the environmental review process normally done under NEPA (or get broad new exemptions from it), approve water projects to improve grazing, and share or keep grazing fee revenue. A state commission dominated by governor appointees—including ranchers and livestock industry representatives—would adopt the management plans. The bill never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers holding federal grazing permits and leases, and the livestock industry generally, gain the most: states sympathetic to grazing would run the program, issue 30-year permits, control environmental review, and could charge their own additional fees while federal fees stay capped. Governors and state agriculture agencies gain authority over federal land within their borders.

how_it_helps.text: At a governor's request, states would administer grazing allotments on BLM and Forest Service land, issuing 30-year grazing permits and leases whose terms are set by a state commission.

States could take over the federal environmental review duties under NEPA for grazing plans, and a long list of grazing-related activities (vegetation treatment, fencing, water infrastructure, changing livestock numbers or seasons) would be categorically excluded from environmental review.

States would assume federal authority to approve and build water infrastructure for grazing, with federal agencies required to provide access and barred from conditioning management on actions affecting water rights.

The state commission that oversees the program would include 11 governor-appointed members out of 14, including several grazing permit holders and representatives of the livestock industry, with only one conservation or environmental seat.

analysis.who_pays: Members of the public who use and value federal lands: they would face grazing decisions made by state commissions where ranching and agriculture representatives hold most appointed seats, with weakened environmental review and fewer avenues to challenge decisions. Federal taxpayers could also bear costs if the fee-sharing arrangement shortchanged the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets states take over federal environmental review duties for grazing plans, or limits federal lead agencies' process with state agricultural agencies as cooperating agencies, and automatically categorically excludes grazing-related vegetation work, fencing, water infrastructure, and grazing changes from environmental review.

State commissions would be dominated by grazing interests: 11 of 14 members are appointed by the governor, including multiple rancher and livestock-promotion seats, with only one conservation representative and three federal appointees, and commissions adopt or approve the management plans.

The bill bars the Interior Board of Land Appeals from hearing challenges to state grazing decisions, limits court fee awards to outside challengers, and makes the state dispute process the route for disagreements.

Grazing permits issued by states would run 30 years with terms set by the state commission, and federal renewal of the cooperative agreement is nearly automatic once monitoring shows positive outcomes, locking in state control for decades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is not fiscal but democratic: the federal public lands involved belong to all Americans, and the bill would hand their day-to-day grazing management to state commissions dominated by ranchers and agriculture interests, with fee caps, long 30-year terms, relaxed environmental review, and limited outside legal recourse. The monitoring and consent requirements temper this somewhat, but the design clearly tilts toward permit holders. It never received a vote, so these tradeoffs were never tested legislatively.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee after introduction, got a subcommittee hearing, and never came to a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the State Grazing Management Authority Act in the Senate on April 19, 2021.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where it remained.
On October 19, 2021, the committee's Public Lands, Forests, and Mining subcommittee held a hearing on the bill.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and public-lands users who favor uniform federal grazing rules, since the transfer of authority never happened; the bill's livestock-industry beneficiaries gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal-oversight status quo; no one changed

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

for.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on October 19, 2021, but took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors, so no meaningful coalition formed on either side.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers and grazing permit holders
industries.note: The bill shifts control of federal grazing allotments to state commissions where ranchers hold several of 14 seats, extends permits to 30-year terms, caps federal fee levels, and lets states charge their own additional fees. This reduces federal oversight over the public forage they use.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (BLM, Forest Service)
industries.note: The agencies would cede day-to-day management, environmental review, water infrastructure approval, and enforcement to states, retaining only termination rights for noncompliance and wildfire-cost recovery.

Grazing-related activities would be categorically excluded from NEPA review and state dispute processes would replace the Interior Board of Land Appeals, limiting avenues for conservation challenges. One conservation seat on each commission is the bill's main concession.
